raw_case_text:
A 72-year-old female presented to our orthopedic outpatient department with pain and deformity in her left lower limb and an inability to bear weight that had persisted for the last six months. Her medical history was insignificant; she had never received steroid/chemotherapy treatment. There was no history of a precipitating injury, surgical intervention, or substance abuse. The patient had no primary immunodeficiency, neutropenia, or chronic granulomatous disease history. She had intermittent fever but denied any gross loss of appetite or weight. She had received treatment for pain and fever from a local practitioner but never visited an expert care center. The treatment prescribed by the practitioner was in the form of two tablets (tramadol and calcium), which the patient had taken twice daily for the last two months. The patient had the prescription record.
Upon clinical examination, the patient had an average build. Physical examination revealed tenderness, mild swelling, and a deformity on the left proximal thigh. The overlying skin appeared smooth and shiny, without scarring or sinus discharge. Palpation revealed tenderness and crepitus of the proximal thigh.
Radiographs of the pelvis, including both hips and left thigh, showed multiple areas of osteolysis in the proximal femur, with gross deformation and cortical breach. There were no noticeable periosteal reactions or soft tissue components (Figure 1). The chest radiograph was normal.
The patient was hospitalized, routine blood investigations were performed, and the results were within normal limits, except for a slightly elevated erythrocyte sedimentation rate of 38 mm/hour (range, 0-20 mm/hour) and a C-reactive protein level of 29 mg/L (range, <5.0 mg/L). Human immunodeficiency virus, hepatitis A, B, C, and E statuses were negative, and serum immunoglobulin and other blood tests were also normal.
Magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) was performed, and it demonstrated multiple rounded T1- and T2-weighted hypointense and short tau inversion recovery (STIR) hyperintense lesions scattered in the lumbar fourth vertebra and mid and distal shaft of the left femur and bilaterally in the pelvic bones and proximal femurs. A large heterogeneous T1- and T2-weighted hypointense and STIR hyperintense lesion involving the left proximal femur, neck, intertrochanteric region, and proximal shaft, with areas of cortical break and periosseous soft tissue edema, were observed (Figures 2-4).
A core biopsy was then performed under local anesthesia. The bone specimens were sent for histopathological examination, Gram staining, acid-fast staining, and culture. Gram staining showed no bacteria and Ziehl-Neelsen staining was negative for acid-fast bacilli. Bacterial cultures for both pyogenic and acid-fast bacteria were negative. Still, gray-green velvety colonies with a narrow white border grew on potato dextrose agar, confirming the presence of Aspergillus fumigatus.
Histopathological specimens showed necrotic bone in hematoxylin and eosin-stained sections, inflammatory granulation tissue, and narrow-branching septate hyphae. After periodic acid-Schiff staining, branching septate fungal hyphae and necrotic bone were also observed. Gomori methenamine silver (GMS)-stained sections revealed the characteristic grayish-black branching septate hyphae of aspergillosis (Figure 5).
Based on the microbiological and histopathological evidence, a final diagnosis of Aspergillus osteomyelitis was made. Blood tests like the Aspergillus galactomannan test and beta-d-glucan test and advanced testing by genome sequencing to differentiate between various Aspergillus species still need to be done due to the non-availability of these modalities in our institute.
After discussions with an infectious disease consultant, antifungal treatment was initiated to first control the extensive spread, and surgical management was planned depending on the response to antifungal treatment. Intravenous amphotericin B (1 mg/kg/day) and oral voriconazole (200 mg every 12 hours) were initiated after baseline renal and liver function tests and electrocardiogram (ECG) were performed. The patient values and reference levels are shown in Table 1. The patient weighed 65 kg, and 65 mg of lyophilized amphotericin B (reconstituted with 10 mL sterile water supplied with the vials) was intravenously administered daily for two weeks in 500 mL of 5% dextrose solution over 3 hours after administering a test dose of 20 mL before the first dose. Therapeutic drug monitoring (TDM) for voriconazole was not performed because this capability was unavailable at our institute. The Aspergillus galactomannan antigen and beta-D-glucan tests were also not performed because of non-availability. However, with the worsening of the coronavirus disease 2019 (COVID-19) pandemic, the patient was discharged upon request, receiving oral voriconazole (200 mg twice daily for three months) and skin traction. Regular telephone consultations and monthly outpatient department visits were also conducted. Routine complete blood count, ECG, and renal and liver function test results were within normal range after two months of follow-up. After 2.5 months of ongoing treatment, the patient died of COVID-19, and a post-mortem was not undertaken.

subjective.chief_complaint: A 72-year-old immunocompetent female presented with a 6-month history of left lower limb pain, proximal thigh deformity, inability to bear weight, and intermittent fever.
subjective.history_of_present_illness: Over the preceding 6 months, the patient experienced progressive left proximal thigh pain, deformity, inability to bear weight, and intermittent fevers without trauma or prior surgery. She had taken oral tramadol and calcium twice daily prescribed by a local practitioner for the past 2 months without improvement.
subjective.past_medical_history: Unremarkable past medical history; no history of corticosteroid or chemotherapy use, trauma, surgery, substance abuse, primary immunodeficiency, neutropenia, or chronic granulomatous disease.
subjective.review_of_systems: Positive for left thigh pain, deformity, inability to bear weight, and intermittent fever; negative for appetite loss or significant weight loss. Pre-admission medications: tramadol and calcium twice daily for 2 months.

objective.physical_examination: Average build; local exam of the left proximal thigh revealed mild swelling, gross deformity, tenderness, and bony crepitus on palpation, with smooth, shiny overlying skin and no scars or draining sinuses.
objective.routine_investigations: Routine CBC, renal and liver function tests, serum immunoglobulins, ECG, and chest radiograph were normal. ESR was elevated at 38 mm/hour (reference 0-20 mm/hour) and CRP was elevated at 29 mg/L (reference <5.0 mg/L). HIV and hepatitis A, B, C, and E serologies were negative. Pelvis and left thigh radiographs showed multiple osteolytic lesions in the left proximal femur with gross deformation and cortical breach without periosteal reaction or soft-tissue mass.
objective.advanced_workup: MRI of the spine, pelvis, and femurs demonstrated a large heterogeneous T1/T2-hypointense, STIR-hyperintense lesion involving the left femoral neck, intertrochanteric region, and proximal shaft with cortical breach and periosseous soft-tissue edema, plus multiple rounded lesions in the L4 vertebra, mid/distal left femoral shaft, and bilateral pelvic bones and proximal femurs. Core bone biopsy under local anesthesia was negative on Gram stain, Ziehl-Neelsen AFB stain, and bacterial/mycobacterial cultures, but potato dextrose agar culture grew gray-green velvety colonies with a narrow white border confirmed as Aspergillus fumigatus. Bone biopsy histopathology (H&E, PAS, and GMS stains) demonstrated necrotic bone, inflammatory granulation tissue, and characteristic grayish-black narrow-branching septate fungal hyphae.

assessment_and_plan.assessment_and_confirmation: Multifocal primary Aspergillus fumigatus osteomyelitis of the left proximal femur, pelvis, and L4 vertebra in an immunocompetent host, definitively confirmed by bone core biopsy histopathology (H&E, PAS, and GMS staining showing branching septate hyphae invading necrotic bone) and fungal culture growing A. fumigatus (pyogenic and mycobacterial osteomyelitis ruled out). Treated with intravenous lyophilized amphotericin B (1 mg/kg/day, 65 mg/day for 2 weeks) and oral voriconazole (200 mg every 12 hours) alongside skin traction, with normal CBC, ECG, and hepatic/renal function at 2-month follow-up; however, 2.5 months into treatment, the patient died of intercurrent COVID-19.
